title: Juniper and the Harvest
premise: Oscar Ravensworth, a hospice nurse who has spent three years hearing the dying count backwards toward zero, returns to the village of Juniper Hollow to settle their late aunt's estate. There they discover the family curse: every generation, the melted church bell rings, and those who hear it are counted down to their deaths unless someone takes their place. As Oscar's own countdown begins, they fall for Wren, the village gravedigger who has cheated the bell twice by hiding among the dead. In the end Oscar realizes the bell doesn't demand a life — it demands an identity — and by surrendering their name and memory to the bell, they break the count forever, waking as a stranger loved by Wren but unknown even to themselves.
about_author: Ada Ishikawa is a former palliative care volunteer from coastal Oregon who writes horror about the tenderness required at the edge of death. She lives with her partner and an elderly one-eyed cat named Vespers.

chapters.title: The Backwards Numbers
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. At the hospice, a dying woman counts down from thirty and stops breathing at zero; Oscar hears it happen again that night in another room. They tell themselves it's coincidence, grief-shaped pattern recognition. The emotional beat is quiet dread — the reader learns Oscar's gift and their three-year habit of rationalizing it.

chapters.title: Juniper Hollow
chapters.summary: Oscar arrives to clear out Aunt Maren's cottage and finds her journals full of tallies, dates, and the phrase 'the bell keeps the books.' A neighbor warns them to leave before Sunday. The beat is unease deepening into invitation: Oscar stays, telling themselves it's just estate paperwork.

chapters.title: A Ring Without Metal
chapters.summary: At dawn the church bell rings — though parish records confirm it was melted for scrap in 1911. Only Oscar and a handful of villagers react; everyone else hears nothing. Oscar meets Wren, the gravedigger, who goes pale at the sound. The beat is the point of no return: the impossible made communal.

chapters.title: What Wren Digs
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren reveals the family curse: the Ravensworths' pact bought the village prosperity, paid in generational lives, counted down by the bell. Wren survived two counts by lying in open graves during the ringing. The beat is reluctant intimacy — two people sharing secrets neither wanted spoken aloud.

chapters.title: The Family Ledger
chapters.summary: Oscar decodes Aunt Maren's journals: names, dates, and countdowns matching hospice memories going back decades. They realize the dying they've heard were all Ravensworth kin or their substitutes. The beat is horrified comprehension — Oscar's whole career has been eavesdropping on the curse.

chapters.title: Nine Days
chapters.summary: The bell rings again, and this time Oscar hears numbers under the tolling: nine days. Wren proposes fleeing together, but the curse follows blood, not geography — Oscar's cousin Delia and her children live in the village and won't leave their livelihoods. The beat is love against duty taking shape as a real choice.

chapters.title: Substitutes
chapters.summary: Wren confesses how they cheated the count twice: strangers died in their place, drawn by the bell. Oscar, a nurse who has spent a life easing death, recoils — then catches themselves calculating who could be spared. The beat is moral vertigo; survival starts looking like something Oscar swore never to do.

chapters.title: Delia's Zero
chapters.summary: Delia's countdown ends early; she dies at her kitchen table mid-sentence, and her children begin counting too. Oscar tries the hospice trick of sitting with them, willing the numbers slower, and it works — briefly. The beat is desperate agency: love can stall the bell but not silence it.

chapters.title: The Bell Keeps the Books
chapters.summary: In the ruined belfry, Oscar finds the original pact carved into the beam: the bell doesn't want lives, it wants names — identities fed to it so the dead can keep living them. Wren begs Oscar to run; instead Oscar climbs toward the bell as the final toll builds. The beat is sacrificial clarity.

chapters.title: A Stranger Named Wren's Love
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The last toll falls silent mid-count. The children stop counting; the village exhales. Oscar wakes in the cottage with no name, no past, no memory of Wren — but alive, and somehow still gentle. Wren chooses to introduce themselves again. The beat is bittersweet resolution: survival purchased with identity, love beginning over from zero.
